newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway govt proposes legal change for bank merger.
newsitem.headline: Norway govt proposes legal change for bank merger.

text.p: The Norwegian government proposed on Tuesday to change legal guidelines in order for it to potentially endorse a proposed merger between Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse ASA and Storebrand ASA.

Christiania, Norway's second biggest bank, and Storebrand, the country's largest insurance company, announced plans in April to merge by the end of 1997 provided they win approval by shareholders and the finance ministry, the regulatory body.

The ministry, in the revised 1997 national budget unveiled on Tuesday, said it could not endorse the merger under current parliamentary guidelines, which say the government for national strategic reasons must hold at least 50 percent of the top banks.

"We have not taken a position on the merger," Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg told a news conference. "We cannot say today if the merger will take place....But we want to have the freedom to say yes or no. With today's rules the government must say no."

The government now holds just over 50 percent of shares in the top commercial banks Den Norske Bank ASA (DnB) ) and Christiania respectively. They were bailed out by the government during a financial crisis between 1988 and 92.
If Christiania and Storebrand merge, the shareholding of the State Bank Investment Fund (SBIF) in Christiania would be watered down to about 25 percent.

"The government holds the view that it is unfortunate that the guidelines of today do not provide a basis for considering whether a merger would be compatible with stable national ownership and business reasons," the ministry said. "The government believes the guidelines must therefore be changed."
The merger, if approved, would form the country's largest financial group and the sixth biggest in the Nordic region.

The Labour minority government has said the state's share may be reduced to 33 percent in Christiania and DnB in the next legislature because so-called negative control may also be controlled at that level.
The next parliamentary elections are in September.
But the finance ministry indicated it might be enough for the government to hold less than 33 percent of the stock and still be able to block unwanted changes in the banks.
"The ownership stake should be large enough to command control through about one-third of the votes at the annual general meeting of a possibly merged financial institution," the ministry said.

"A diverse ownership structure could allow for negative control through a lower ownership stake than one-third because it is known from experience that a diverse ownership means a lower percentage of shareholders are represented at the annual general meeting." --Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41
